title: Nehemiah's wall (Nehemiah 2–4)
hookLine: a cupbearer weeps, prays, and rebuilds with a trowel in one hand and a sword in the other
carry: let us rise up and build

cards: Nehemiah has a good job. He's cupbearer to the king of Persia, the man who hands the king his wine. Then visitors arrive from Judah, and he asks how Jerusalem is doing.
Badly: the wall is broken down and the gates are burned. Nehemiah writes: "I sat down and wept, and mourned certain days, and fasted, and prayed before the God of heaven."
Later, as he serves the wine, the king notices his face. Why is your face sad, when you're not sick? Nehemiah is frightened.
He's about to ask for something enormous.

teach.b: The king asks what he wants, and Nehemiah writes: "So I prayed to the God of heaven." No time for a long prayer. A breath of one, between a question and an answer, standing beside the throne.
Then: send me to rebuild the city. And the king says yes. In Jerusalem, Nehemiah doesn't start with a speech.

teach.h: A NIGHT RIDE AROUND THE RUINS.
teach.b: He rides out at night with a few men to see the ruins for himself. Only then does he gather the people and tell them what he saw and how God had helped him.
Their answer: "Let us rise up and build. So they strengthened their hands for this good work."
Chapter three is a long list of names and gates: families, priests, goldsmiths, apothecaries, some repairing the section by their own house. Then the mocking starts.
Sanballat and Tobiah, local officials who oppose the work, laugh at it. Tobiah's joke is in the text: "even that which they build, if a fox go up, he shall even break down their stone wall."

teach.h: ONE HAND WORKS, ONE HOLDS A WEAPON.
teach.b: The mocking turns into threats of attack, so Nehemiah sets guards, and the builders change how they work: "Every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon."

They kept building anyway. Some Christians read this as a picture of steady work under pressure: pray in a breath, look at the damage honestly, build your own stretch, and don't stop because someone is laughing.

how: Christians sometimes read Nehemiah when a church or community starts a building or repair project, and some take up his quick prayer between two sentences as a model for praying in the middle of a hard conversation.

games.q: you're Nehemiah, serving wine. the king asks why you look sad and what you want. the answer could cost you everything. what do you do?
o: say it's nothing and keep pouring.
pray to the God of heaven, then ask to go and rebuild.
ask for a week to think about it.
games.why: "So I prayed to the God of heaven," and then he asks to be sent to Jerusalem. the king says yes.

practice: Like Nehemiah riding out at night, look honestly at one thing that's broken, a friendship, a habit, a room, a promise you didn't keep, and see the damage clearly without blaming anyone.
Then find one stretch, the small section by your own house, that you could repair. If you pray, pray to the God of heaven in a breath, the way Nehemiah did; if you don't, just name the stretch.

wordCard.voice: Nehemiah's wall. Jerusalem's broken wall, rebuilt by builders each working their own stretch, with one hand on the work and the other on a weapon.

orig.note: Hebrew: let us rise up and build, the people's answer in Nehemiah 2:18.

carryVoice: Your line: let us rise up and build. From a muddy river to an opened eye, a lost book, an exile, a queen's courage, a foundation and a wall, it was a week of building. Rest well.
